speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: asked the Minister for Manpower in light of the need to attract top global talent for key sectors in Singapore (a) whether there are initiatives to bring top overseas Singaporean talent back to Singapore; (b) what is the success rate in attracting top overseas Singaporeans to relocate and work in key sectors in Singapore; and (c) whether there is support to help top overseas Singaporean talent and their families to relocate and transition back in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) what is the success rate in growing our local manpower talent for the key sectors in Singapore; and (b) whether there is data to show that Singaporeans are succeeding in getting quality jobs in these key sectors.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: asked the Minister for Manpower whether the Ministry has any plans to impose personal responsibility on human resource professionals in Singapore to comply with all manpower rules and regulations, such as the Fair Consideration Framework and Complementarity Assessment Framework.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) for organisations that have made job postings on the Government's MyCareersFuture portal, whether they are required to notify the Ministry on the outcome of a job posting when it is subsequently delisted or when the role is filled; (b) if so, do the numbers suggest that ample efforts have been made to give fair consideration to local candidates; and (c) if not, why not.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members of the House, I delivered a Ministerial Statement last month on “Strengthening Singapore’s Position as a Global Hub for Talent”.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In the Statement, I outlined how we intend to strengthen Singapore’s position as a global hub for talent and addressed questions around the enhancement of our work pass framework, including the introduction of the Overseas Networks & Expertise (ONE) Pass.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members have subsequently filed a number of Parliamentary Questions on three related issues.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, on how we ensure a complementary foreign workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Second, on our concurrent efforts to develop our local talent pipeline.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And last but not least, on our efforts to safeguard fair consideration.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I am taking them together, so that we can address the issues more holistically.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I will address questions which are more technical in nature on specific policies separately.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First and foremost, ensuring a complementary foreign workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members in this House generally acknowledge the need to attract top talent, as per the intent of the ONE Pass.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Some Members have, however, raised questions on our broader foreign workforce policy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the Employment Pass (EP) level, we focus on ensuring that the EP holders are of good quality.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To answer Mr Gerald Giam’s question on whether there are plans to review the EP framework to introduce a quota for the bottom half of income earners among EP holders, we have explained our rationale before – doing so will restrict our ability to compete and hold our companies back.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our emphasis on quality was reinforced when the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) announced significant adjustments to our EP framework at this year’s Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Companies whose candidates cannot meet the EP qualifying salary or pass COMPASS will have to apply for an S Pass instead, where they will be subject to a quota.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is a neater solution than what Mr Giam is suggesting.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Compared to his suggestion where some EP holders are subjected to a quota while others are not, our current approach has the merit of keeping the positioning and criteria of each pass type clear, and overall work pass framework simpler for businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Being open and connected and bringing in complementary global talent have helped to grow the overall pie for Singapore and more good job opportunities for locals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Jessica Tan asked if there is data to show that Singaporeans are succeeding in getting quality jobs in key sectors.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the same time, Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked about the number of EP holders in the Information and Communications sector, compared to other sectors.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Information and Communications sector has been a fast-growing one and is a sector that is facing talent shortages worldwide.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In Singapore and elsewhere, employers have had to tap into the global marketplace for skills in shortages.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This has increased from one-sixth in 2016, thus reflecting the growing digital needs of our economy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The growth of the Information and Communications sector has also resulted in creation of more jobs for our locals – in the same timeframe, we saw strong growth in the number of local PMETs by 34,400.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Median local wages in the sector also continue to increase.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Therefore, we can see quite clearly that it is not a zero-sum game.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the macro level, the data is also encouraging.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There are more locals in higher-skilled PMET jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Across the board, local workers have experienced sustained wage growth.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The median income of full-time employed residents has grown from $4,100 to $4,700 over the same period, an increase of 2.1% per annum in real terms.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have also seen improved job quality and better wages at the lower end, with the income of full-time employed residents at the 20th percentile increasing 2.7% per annum in real terms over the same period.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai also filed a question in a subsequent Sitting specifically on local postgraduates, a group that is very likely to be taking up or even creating these high-quality roles.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Their average unemployment rate has remained lower than that of all locals over the past five years.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have managed to create good employment outcomes because we continue to be an attractive place for companies to do business.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: By combining and complementing local and foreign expertise, we can attract more investments and create many more good job and career choices for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Conversely, if companies do not have access to the complementary foreign manpower that they need, they may exit Singapore and take the jobs they create for Singaporeans with them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When it comes to foreign workforce policies, the way to advance is to strike a very careful and delicate balance.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Next, on developing our local talent pool and workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Local talent development already happens organically in tandem with economic growth.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As businesses expand their investments here, they will need to find manpower to fill various roles and invest in training and upgrading their workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: By working in leading firms and alongside global talent, our local workers will also gain exposure to new ideas and best practices from around the world.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Government and tripartite partners help to catalyse this process.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We work with industry stakeholders to chart out transformation plans across 23 sectors through the Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs), which include strategies to prepare our workers for higher value-added jobs in each sector.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have also put in place a whole eco-system of programmes and schemes which businesses can tap on to prepare their workers for jobs of the future.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Employers can also tap on subsidised industry-relevant training courses and reskilling programmes for mid-career workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This includes Workforce Singapore (WSG)’s Career Conversion Programmes (CCPs).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar1 filed a question for a later Sitting on how work experience and other certifications are considered aside from formal academic qualifications in eligibility requirements for CCPs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For some CCPs, academic requirements are put in place to ensure that the trainee is able to cope with the training, particularly where the training is very technical in nature.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Applicants who do not meet the academic requirements may still be accepted into the programme if they have relevant alternative qualifications or work experience.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Jessica Tan also asked about our initiatives to bring back top overseas Singaporean talent.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Overseas Singaporeans, who have developed the ability to thrive in a global environment or who have gained industry-relevant experience and built extensive networks, can make significant contributions to our economy and pass on their knowledge to other Singaporean talent.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Fundamentally, strengthening Singapore’s position as a global hub for talent which is brimming with exciting opportunities is self-reinforcing – it will help to bring back overseas Singaporeans who are keen to contribute and to be a part of this ecosystem.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Government actively engages overseas Singaporeans to keep them connected to home, so that they can make an informed decision about whether and when to return to Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Singapore Global Network (SGN) within the Economic Development Board (EDB) plays a key role in broadening and deepening our overseas Singaporean network through digital engagement, as well as partnerships with private, public and community organisations to deliver engagement initiatives, such as networking and community events.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These engagements also allow overseas Singaporeans to serve as our valuable connectors and ambassadors in overseas markets, helping to spread Singapore's good reputation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For returning Singaporeans, SGN and other agencies offer a variety of online resources to facilitate a smooth transition, including information on education, working and living, as well as relocating back home to Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For example, the Ministry of Education (MOE)'s website contains information about school admissions for returning Singaporean children.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There is no place for discrimination in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: MOM does not and will not tolerate unfair hiring practices and employers who do not give locals a fair chance will face stiff penalties.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Fair Consideration Framework (FCF) sets out requirements for all employers to consider local workers fairly for job opportunities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the number of companies placed on the FCF watchlist.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Firms are placed on the FCF watchlist if they have an exceptionally high share of foreign PMETs compared to their industry peers, or a high concentration of a single foreign nationality source.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But, Members of the House, let me reiterate this.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Firms placed on the FCF watchlist have not flouted any rules.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Instead, what the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) does is to engage these companies to help them improve their workforce profiles.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: One other limb of FCF is the job advertising requirement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Employers must first advertise on MyCareersFuture (MCF) and fairly consider all candidates, before submitting an EP or S Pass application.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Louis Chua asked whether companies need to notify MOM on the outcome of a job posting when it is subsequently delisted or when the role is filled.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We do not require companies to do so, just like how they also do not need to do so for other job portals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are conscious of the fact that we should not add administrative burden and make it onerous for employers to use MCF.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: While the number of cases of discriminatory practices is small, MOM will continue to remain vigilant.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Besides investigating complaints lodged with TAFEP, we will also use data analytics to identify suspicious cases for further investigation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And where employers are found to be discriminatory, MOM will not hesitate to take action against such employers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The regulatory actions included issuance of warning and being barred from hiring or renewing foreign workers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Hazel Poa also asked whether MOM intends to impose personal responsibility on human resource (HR) professionals in Singapore to comply with all manpower rules and regulations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Senior management as well as line managers are also involved in these hiring decisions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This includes HR professionals as well as business leaders.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Employers, business leaders and HR professionals all play an important role in ensuring that their companies' employment practices are fair and that they comply with regulations and the Tripartite Guidelines.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Beyond enforcement, we must also enable and equip HR professionals to better support their companies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: One is with regards to the quality of jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Minister shared about the make-up of Singaporeans and residents and our workers in Singapore, in terms of the PMET jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Could he also share if there is any data, in that same vein, for leadership roles as the development has happened of Singaporeans taking up professional leadership roles in these sectors?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The other supplementary question I have – it is very heartening to hear about the outreach on SGN and keeping in contact with Singaporeans overseas.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Specifically, with regards to top talent for the key sectors that we are focusing on, what specific actions or initiatives are being done to engage and attract top talent back to Singapore to be able to fill those key positions, as we look at attracting foreign talents and specific support to their families in terms of transitioning, especially if they have non-Singaporeans as spouses?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the leadership roles, we do not have the data available at hand today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, perhaps, that would give you some form of a broad macro indicator, if you take that as a proxy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But, like I said, it may not necessarily be an accurate proxy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the top talent in many of these key sectors that we talked about, we have a significant number of initiatives that we have put in place to try to bring them back.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: While I agree with Ms Jessica Tan that returning top Singaporean talent can make significant contributions to our economy back home, where they are in today, in many of the tier one cities all over the world, they can also serve as valuable connectors and advocates in many of these overseas markets while they continue to gain the networks, the expertise and the industry relevant experiences abroad.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Many of them actually chose to carry on staying for longer periods because they have got other ties, work commitments, maybe friends and schools.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The initiatives that we have started, I could give you a few examples.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is co-organised by the Institute of Banking and Finance (IBF), SGN and the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We held the inaugural forum in May 2022.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It was a two-day event featuring insights from industry leaders on key growth areas and career opportunities in Singapore's financial centre.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The people who attended felt that it was a very good forum for them to communicate and also for them to consider relocating back home and included fireside chat with industry leaders on their overseas experiences and relocation journeys as well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This seeks to attract outstanding overseas based Singaporean research leaders back to Singapore to take up leadership positions in our universities and our research institutions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: NRF has been engaging our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) as well as the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR) to identify some of these suitable candidates.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This way employers can be incentivised to hire and train Singaporeans to fill those positions when the EP expires and there will be more knowledge and skills transferred to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is a proposal that the Member for Aljunied Group Representation Constituency (GRC) Leon Perera raised in October 2020.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, with the COMPASS framework, a candidate can attain a passing score even with zero points on the diversity criterion, which in any case is quite low because it looks only at the share of the candidates' own nationality among the firm's PMETs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will ensure that companies give consideration to all the criteria and ensure a more level playing field for Singaporean PMETs during the hiring process.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, on the Employment Pass, we have earlier on said that there is no fixed-term EP.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In fact, the EP holders for these companies, they do not enjoy an automatic renewal for these EP holders.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There is a certain validity and some of them are on a two-year term, some are on a one-year term and subject to companies renewing them, subject to other criteria, these EPs are not automatically renewed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think these are important points to take note of.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are reviewing and getting feedback still from the industry.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I am looking at some of the criteria to see how we can nuance it to make sure that not only is it business-friendly, but that they can continue to help us achieve our desired end game of levelling up the opportunities for our Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, we are in a very tight labour market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Any introduction of any new policy to nuance this framework would be viewed as further tightening.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I hope the Member understands the delicate situation and the fine balance that we are in.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Two of the characteristics pertain to the individual characteristics; and two, relate to the firm.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think it is sufficient for now to move ahead with this framework and let it run.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Does MOM have investigatory powers to ascertain whether a company did the FCF job advertising in bad faith?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For example, whether a company has already decided on a foreign candidate beforehand?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My second supplementary question is, whether MOM will consider calibrating the FCF or watchlist into tiers, with a specific tier where firms are named and identified.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As I have shared earlier on, MOM today has various tools, including data analytics to look into firms, which hire in bad faith.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I would not be able to share at length or in-depth what some of these predictive analytics are, because by sharing them, we then got to keep inventing newer and better AI tools to identify them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, the vast majority of the firms under the FCF watchlist, when we work with them to improve some of their hiring practices and policies, the majority of them end up exiting the watchlist.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: From the data of such policies that are available today, do not seem to indicate that this is a pervasive problem.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There will always be outliers but because the core of what we do is to improve and level up opportunities for our local Singaporean Core, we will continue to nuance our approach to these films.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I refer to the Minister's earlier reply, specifically where he mentioned that companies on the FCF have not actually flouted any rules.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of the Ministry's newly-introduced COMPASS, where diversity is listed as a firm related attribute in considering EP applicants, how significant in the Minister's opinion, would this new criterion be in reducing the number of companies on the FCF watchlist over time?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As I have said earlier on, two of the criteria relate to the individual and two of the criteria relate to the firm.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Because it is almost a set of interlocking gear, whatever you move in one criterion will affect the rest.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our sense today is that, in the run-up to implementing COMPASS and as we engaged more firms, we get feedback that this is a good framework which helps to differentiate our workforce.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It also allows us to review from time to time, how we can be more responsive to the type of jobs and the type of talent our country and our economy needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, directionally, COMPASS is a move in the right direction because it allows us a very differentiated strategy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I note from the Minister's response on the use of data analytics.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Just wondering if the Minister can share with us in terms of the data points that are being collected from companies which make an EP application, to show that they have failed to source for a local candidate after the 14-day or 28-day period, despite their best efforts.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Then, the MOM side can also satisfy itself that this is truly the case for these companies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: MOM would rely on multiple data points to allow us to triangulate.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will vary across the different sectors that we are dealing with.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: One key point that we will consider, obviously, is how acutely short, in terms of the talent that is needed for one particular sector, whether it is in deep tech.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And given the shortage, that is one data point that we would use to consider in terms of our data analytics.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, today, if you look at the outcome, which is a very low long-term unemployment rate, for us to ensure that in a tight labour market, companies can continue to do well, to be able to have access to the manpower that they need to run the operations, we work very closely with them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In the process of working with them, we also identify certain characteristics and behaviour that allow us to develop these analytics.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope that gives Members a broad perspective of what we are doing.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister mentioned earlier that they can already take action on individuals for non-compliance.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on what kind of actions can be taken on these individuals?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And which legislation is this power conferred under?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Today, MOM works very closely with the Institute for HR Professionals (IHRP), as well as our tripartite partners and employees to professionalise the HR workforce and to strengthen HR practices and capabilities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: One key effort is the IHRP certification, which recognises the level of skills and experience of HR professionals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Incumbent within the process certification, it assesses the knowledge and the understanding of our employment legislation and regulations, including FCF well as the soon to be implemented COMPASS.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do not want to go too much into the details of that training.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: All certified HR professionals must comply with the IHRP's code of professional conduct.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: They can also suspend the certification or permanently bar the individual from being certified, depending on the severity of the breach.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Employers who are convicted of false declaration under the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act will face imprisonment of up to two years or fine of up to $20,000, or both.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And how can we make sure that in a world where more and more people are going for certifications and training, that these are not cast aside when they apply for career conversion programmes or even jobs?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members of the House and Ms Mariam Jaafar would appreciate the wide diaspora of jobs and skillsets that are needed to fulfil the roles.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There will be very, very clear cut roles, which would require say, understanding of arithmetic, or even physics.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Because safety of certain work process is needed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I recently dealt with an appeal, filed by a Member here, appealing for a particular resident to be given an exemption from having to pass certain tests.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But because this pertains to workplace safety where a basic understanding of the calculation of the weight-bearing nature of certain platforms and tensile strength of the rope is necessary.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, a basic understanding of physics is therefore needed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: That could not be substituted by just experience or some other alternative qualifications.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And if not, try to find an alternative role to place the person in.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I guess the very long answer to the Member's question is that it is very difficult for us to be able to substitute away every single skill by an alternative qualification.
